savvy

SAV-ee — a savvy person 'has' the practical know-how to handle things well. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Savvy is shrewd and knowledgeable, especially about practical matters.

The savvy negotiator knew exactly when to walk away from the table to get a better deal.

Example

Before buying a used car, a savvy shopper researches its exact model online, checks its full repair history, and brings a mechanic friend along to inspect the engine before ever speaking to the salesperson.

Being practically knowledgeable enough to avoid getting cheated is what makes the shopper savvy. Unlike 'lucky,' which is about chance, savvy is about genuine skill and awareness.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

astute: Astute means having keen insight — an astute reader sees what a writer only implies. It praises sharp perception anywhere, including books and theory. Savvy is more hands-on: practical know-how about how things really work, picked up by doing rather than studying.

canny: Canny means clever and careful, especially about money and deals — a canny shopper never overpays, and there is always a cautious, penny-watching edge to it. Savvy is broader practical smarts and carries no special note of caution or thrift.

street-smart: Street-smart means wised-up by real life in tough or busy places — knowing whom to trust and when to walk away. Savvy covers the same practical intelligence but ranges wider: a person can be tech savvy or business savvy without ever leaving an office.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

naive: lacking experience or worldly wisdom

clueless: having no understanding or awareness

Where it sits · how cleverly knowledge gets put to use

informed → savvy → shrewd

informed vs. savvy: Informed is weaker than savvy — being informed just means you have facts, while being savvy means you know how to use that knowledge cleverly in practical situations.

shrewd vs. savvy: Shrewd can feel sharper than savvy: both describe practical smarts, but shrewd often implies an even sharper, sometimes calculating edge to that knowledge.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sav-/sap-: to know, to be wise (Latin (sapere), via French/Creole savez)

Put it together: Savvy traces back to Latin sapere, 'to be wise, to know,' passed into English through a French/Creole phrase meaning 'you know.' At its root, being savvy means genuinely knowing what you're doing.

Use the root in a new word: sage: In the story, the hero crosses two deserts searching for a sage.
